title: Schools, Hebrew Learning, and the Making of a Jewish Future in Będzin
summary: Education was a major communal undertaking, spanning traditional religious instruction, Hebrew schooling, and the ambitious Jewish gymnasium.

editorialContent:
![Będzin, the town whose Jewish schools served children from across Zagłębie](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/11/B%C4%99dzin_-_Zamek_obronny_z_XIVw..jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=api&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)

## A school imagined amid war

Będzin’s Jewish educational world was not one school but several answers to a question: what should a Jewish child learn, and for what future? The memorial book remembers traditional religious study, modern communal schools, Hebrew classes, and institutions shaped by different political and religious commitments. Their histories overlap, but they were not interchangeable.

The book’s account of Yavne’s beginnings varies in its dating. J. Wygodzki recalls that organizers met in **1916** and opened classes the following year; Mordechai Hampel places the first initiative in **1919**. Another memorial-book passage says that activists’ idea arose in 1917, while a separate account identifies Yavne as an educational institution established that year. These recollections may refer to different stages—discussion, authorization, and opening—but the sources do not settle the discrepancy. The safest conclusion is that Yavne emerged from wartime organizing and began teaching in 1917, while some later accounts remember the founding impulse differently. ([J. Wygodzki’s account](/communities/bedzin/records/mention_2865316f71d0e07c099a6da4); [Hampel’s account](/communities/bedzin/records/event_candidate_1279f53973379262d1c972cf))

The school’s founders included Berysz Prager, Jeszaja Hendl Erlich, Salomon Gutman, Mosze Szajn, J. Wigodzki, Majer Potasz, Szymon Zmudzki, and others. Wygodzki remembers permission obtained from the occupying authorities and the first classes at Kołłątaja Street, no. 45. Hampel describes a dual-language Hebrew–Polish school, created partly because families had been sending children to a Christian commercial school for want of a Jewish alternative. Together, their accounts present education as both practical provision and a claim to Jewish communal life. ([Wygodzki](/communities/bedzin/records/mention_2865316f71d0e07c099a6da4); [Hampel](/communities/bedzin/records/event_candidate_1279f53973379262d1c972cf))

## Yavne and the price of a modern education

Yavne combined general studies with Jewish subjects and a strong emphasis on Hebrew. Its early existence was precarious: cramped rented rooms restricted the school’s ability to provide laboratories, a library, recreation space, and physical education. The memorial book’s accounts differ on the personnel and stages of its development. One names Dr. Noach Braun as the first director; another recalls Dr. Braun and later Dr. Fajwel Widerman, while a record associates Salomon Gutman with leadership. These may describe succession or distinct institutional phases, but the recollections should not be flattened into a single unqualified roster. ([Yavne’s early history](/communities/bedzin/records/mention_2865316f71d0e07c099a6da4); [Hampel’s account](/communities/bedzin/records/mention_2865316f71d0e07c099a6da4))

Money repeatedly threatened the school. The memorial book recalls a 1925 crisis serious enough that the supervisory council considered closing it. Gutman pledged annual support and tuition for ten pupils; Chaim and Jicchak Szajn also helped finance students. The record of Shimon Furstenberg (also rendered Fürstenberg and Firstenberg) shows a later, larger intervention: he covered deficits, promised a purpose-built school, and funded a building equipped for instruction and student life. The gymnasium received public rights, an important recognition for a private institution, and moved into Furstenberg’s building at the beginning of the 1929–30 school year. The memorial book remembers the new facilities as including classrooms, laboratories, a library, gymnasium, sports grounds, and swimming pool. ([Furstenberg and the gymnasium](/communities/bedzin/records/mention_9a582448c9c56cf2ba08ad8f); [building and move](/communities/bedzin/records/event_candidate_aac0e64b2ac26b613088bf40))

The institution’s name also changed. Yavne became the coeducational gymnasium of Szymon Fürstenberg and his wife, while another memorial-book chapter describes a Hebrew-Polish gymnasium named for him. The name change did not erase Yavne’s earlier identity: it records how a movement-founded school could become a major regional institution through civic recognition and private philanthropy. Its students came not only from Będzin but from elsewhere in Zagłębie and Upper Silesia. The book recalls Chaim Nachman Bialik visiting in 1931 and praising the school’s educators and committee. ([Bialik’s visit](/communities/bedzin/records/event_candidate_da19b41cd674ba6481123755); [Yavne and the Furstenberg school](/communities/bedzin/records/mention_da349361ca88f503604ff8dc))

## Different needs, different classrooms

Yavne was one educational path, not the whole system. The Mizrahi school began as *Beit Sefer Mizrahi*, founded by religious-national organizers including L. Buchwitz. The memorial book says its enrollment grew rapidly and that it taught both Jewish and general subjects; Hebrew was prominent. It later used the name Yavne too, creating a naming overlap with the gymnasium. The records therefore point to related but distinct institutions and phases: the Mizrahi school and the Yavne gymnasium should not simply be treated as one school. Dr. A. Gatesdiner led the Mizrahi school in 1930–31, according to the book’s account. ([Mizrahi school](/communities/bedzin/records/mention_6e36e7c92a1b5192a79d3178); [Yavne School](/communities/bedzin/records/mention_8494231ffc4b9a92b86dd1b4))

Traditional religious learning remained essential. The memorial book names a Talmud Torah on Zavole Street and recalls efforts to provide clothing for poor pupils. It also describes the cheder moving into a purchased three-story building. These records reveal a communal concern different from the gymnasium’s: sustaining foundational religious education and making it accessible to children whose families had limited means. ([Talmud Torah](/communities/bedzin/records/mention_2434d8d83b9761469b5bdbf7); [Będzin Cheder](/communities/bedzin/records/mention_3d990e08eb8136e559c1fe4b))

Girls’ education had its own institutional expression. A Jewish girls’ school is mentioned in the account of Yavne’s early premises, and Beit Yaakov, founded in Będzin in 1925 and affiliated with Bnot Agudat Israel, offered a religious educational setting for girls. These institutions broaden the picture beyond the boys and coeducational gymnasium most prominent in the surviving school narratives. ([Beit Yaakov](/communities/bedzin/records/mention_58ae380690172f11d92420a2))

## Hebrew beyond the school day

The memorial book also remembers Hebrew as a community project. The local Tarbut association brought together Zionist groups, organized evening classes, and relied on teachers including A. Z. Bornsztajn, Yitzhak Zilbershats, and Yitzhak Fishel of Sosnowiec. Hundreds enrolled, the account says, including people from religious and assimilated families. When space was short, Yavne allowed Tarbut to use classrooms in the evenings. This was a practical partnership: a school’s rooms extended Hebrew learning to adults and other students beyond its formal timetable.

But the book is candid about what did not happen. Będzin had no separate Tarbut school, despite repeated proposals. Its account quotes a 1938 appeal arguing for a Hebrew school whose graduates might continue to the Hebrew University in Jerusalem or the Technion in Haifa. Necha Rotner and WIZO helped establish a Hebrew kindergarten, remembered as a place where children spoke Hebrew. The hoped-for school remained unrealized when the Holocaust destroyed the community. ([Tarbut and Hebrew classes](/communities/bedzin/records/mention_f1eca1e53102f0d26e63ea0a); [WIZO kindergarten](/communities/bedzin/records/mention_75b166296b180b70284514a4))

## A future cut short

The wider record confirms both the scale of Jewish life in Będzin and its violent destruction. The town’s Jewish community was a large part of its population before the war, and German occupation brought persecution, deportation, and the eventual destruction of the community. ([Będzin’s Jewish community](/https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C4%99dzin)) A survivor’s testimony preserved by Yad Vashem states that Będzin’s Jewish schools—including grammar schools, trade and religious schools, and a private coeducational high school—did not reopen after September 1939. Education, as an organized public life, was abruptly ended. ([Yad Vashem, *Stolen Youth*, chapter 2](/https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/pdf-drupal/en/education/stolen_youth2.pdf))

The memorial book’s school stories are therefore more than institutional histories. They preserve the names of organizers, teachers, donors, and pupils, and show how Będzin’s Jews built different educational routes for religious continuity, Hebrew culture, and modern professional opportunity. The records do not establish the later fate of every person named, and the schools’ divergent memories should remain visible. What they make clear is that a Jewish future in Będzin was something people tried to build—in classrooms, evening lessons, a kindergarten, and a gymnasium whose doors opened to children from across the region.
